identity.title: The circumbinary disc of HD 34700A: II. Analysis of a strong dust asymmetry

question.value: Characterise the crescent morphology of the circumbinary disc around HD 34700A and compare it with IRS 48 and HD 142527, discuss their possible origin, and assess the efficiency of dust trapping in the vortex scenario.

evidence.quote: We aim to characterise the crescent morphology, discuss their possible origin, and, in the case of the vortex scenario, assess the efficiency of dust trapping in these systems.
In this work, we consider ALMA band 6 continuum data of the system HD 34700 A (2022.1.00760.S; PI: J. Stadler)
ALMA band 7 ($0.87~\rm mm$) continuum observations of the disc IRS 48 (2019.1.01059.S; PI: H. Yang)
and ALMA band 7 continuum data of the system HD 142527 (2013.1.00305.S; PI: S. Casassus).

analysis_steps.goal: Parametric visibility modelling of circular and eccentric disc morphologies

method.value: Fit 2D parametric brightness models (central/offset Gaussian + Gaussian ring + 1 or 2 asymmetric Gaussian arcs) to visibilities using galario and emcee

evidence.quote: We use the code `galario` (cite: Tazzari_2018) to fit the visibility data and characterize the morphological structure of the continuum emission.
We assume a 2D parametric intensity model and follow a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) approach implemented with the package `emcee` (cite: Foreman-Mackey_2013).
We use the Gaussian to describe the emission originating inside the cavity, the Gaussian ring, and the Gaussian arcs to model the asymmetric ring

key_parameters.value: 15 parameters for HD 34700A, 13 for IRS 48, 23 for HD 142527 (plus eccentricity e and argument of periastron omega for eccentric models)

evidence.quote: The models for HD 34700 A, IRS 48 and HD 142527 have a total of $15$, $13$ and $23$ parameters, respectively.

key_parameters.value: Preliminary run: 100 walkers, ~10^3 steps; Fiducial run: 120 walkers, 2x10^4 steps, 25% burn-in

evidence.quote: As initial step we use 100 walkers over $\sim10^3$ steps.
For each dataset we set up 120 walkers and $2\times10^4$ steps, and discard the first $25\%$ steps as burn-in.

assumptions.value: Inner Gaussian fixed to image centre for HD 34700A; no inner Gaussian for IRS 48; same eccentricity for all ring and arc components in eccentric fits

evidence.quote: We choose to fix the inner Gaussian to the image centre for the HD 34700 A model due to its proximity to the ring asymmetry, as the inner Gaussian would merge with the ring otherwise.
As a result, we choose not to use a Gaussian component in the model of IRS 48.
We fix the eccentricity to be the same for all the ring and arc components in each disc model, and start the fitting procedure using these new parameters.

fitting.value: MCMC with emcee using uniform priors (log-uniform for fluxes, linear for others); narrow priors on i and PA for HD 34700A and IRS 48

evidence.quote: We perform a preliminary exploration of the parameter space with `emcee` using uniform priors, sampling $f_0$, $f_1$, $f_1^a$ and $f_2^a$ logarithmically and the remaining parameters linearly.

validation.value: Checked that unfixing central Gaussian in HD 34700A or allowing wider priors on i and PA keeps parameters within 1 sigma; imaged synthetic model and residual visibilities with tclean

evidence.quote: We check that fixing the Gaussian in the centre does not affect the remaining parameters of the model, as they remain within $1\sigma$ error bars when the Gaussian is not fixed in the centre.
We then image the best fit `galario` model and the residuals using the same procedure explained in Sec. 2.3.
At a later stage, we check that allowing for wider priors does not significantly change the geometrical parameters.

findings_qualitative.value: HD 34700A exhibits a 0.46'' (161 au) dust cavity, unresolved inner disc emission, and an asymmetric ring at 0.53'' (186 au) with a trailing tail and contrast of 62, the second highest contrast detected with ALMA in a protoplanetary disc.

evidence.quote: We detect a $0.46\ensuremath{''}$ ($161~\rm au$) large cavity and resolve a ring with an asymmetric crescent and an extended tail at $0.53\ensuremath{''}$ ($186~\rm au$) with peak intensity of $1.9~\rm mJy beam^{-1}$, corresponding to the second highest contrast ($\sim$62) ever detected with ALMA in a protoplanetary disc.
We also detect unresolved emission inside the cavity, that we attribute to an inner disc.

findings_qualitative.value: The high azimuthal contrast of the asymmetries in HD 34700A, IRS 48, and HD 142527 rules out the orbit clustering of eccentric cavities scenario, while analytical dust trapping and hydrodynamic models support the vortex scenario as plausible.

evidence.quote: The high azimuthal contrast of the asymmetries rules out the orbit clustering of eccentric cavities scenario, while the dust evolution models we consider suggest that the vortex scenario is a plausible option.

findings_qualitative.value: Circular and eccentric visibility models of HD 34700A show no substantial difference in residuals, indicating a degeneracy that leaves it unclear whether the ring is circular or eccentric.

evidence.quote: It is interesting to note that the residuals in both the eccentric and circular models do not show any substantial difference.
This suggests that there is a degeneracy between the circular and eccentric model, and it is currently unclear if the disc around HD 34700 A is circular or eccentric.

claims.hypothesis: A 2D parametric visibility model consisting of a central/offset Gaussian, a Gaussian ring, and one or two asymmetric Gaussian arcs can accurately reproduce the continuum morphology of HD 34700A, HD 142527, and IRS 48.
claims.experiment: Fit ALMA continuum visibilities using galario and emcee for HD 34700A (1 arc), IRS 48 (1 arc, no inner Gaussian), and HD 142527 (2 arcs), and image the residuals.
claims.result: HD 34700A is reproduced with localized residuals up to 7.4 sigma (~2.7% of peak) in the tail; HD 142527 double-peaked ring is recovered with residuals up to 20.1 sigma (6.2% of peak, >6x improvement over previous single-arc model); IRS 48 crescent is recovered (residuals up to 96 sigma / -152 sigma) but the fainter ring is not.
claims.finding: The parametric model agrees remarkably well with HD 34700A and significantly improves the fit for HD 142527, though the tail in HD 34700A and ring in HD 142527/IRS 48 have more complex structure than simple circular Gaussians.

evidence.quote: Our visibility model is in remarkable agreement with the HD 34700A data, featuring only localised residuals in the region of the disc corresponding to the tail of the asymmetry.
For HD 142527, we obtain a very good overall agreement with the data, recovering both the double peaked asymmetric ring and the inner disc emission.
In the case of IRS 48 we recover the general morphology of the asymmetry, but we cannot reproduce the fainter ring.

claims.hypothesis: The high-contrast continuum asymmetries in HD 34700A, IRS 48, and HD 142527 are caused by orbit clustering in an eccentric disc rather than azimuthal dust trapping at a pressure maximum.
claims.experiment: Measure the azimuthal peak-to-average continuum intensity contrast in all three discs and compare with theoretical limits for eccentric orbit clustering (contrast <= 5).
claims.result: Measured azimuthal contrasts are 62 for HD 34700A, 259 for IRS 48, and 37 for HD 142527.
claims.finding: The orbit clustering of eccentric cavities scenario is ruled out by the high azimuthal contrasts.

evidence.quote: As the overdensity is a consequence of the orbits clustering and eccentricity gradient of the disc, it also does not create azimuthal pressure variations and does not trap dust, achieving only a moderate azimuthal contrast of $\lesssim5$ (cite: Ataiee2013).
The high azimuthal contrast of the asymmetries rules out the orbit clustering of eccentric cavities scenario (cite: Ataiee2013).

claims.hypothesis: Dust trapping in an anticyclonic vortex can reproduce the observed azimuthal intensity profile and asymmetric trailing tail of HD 34700A.
claims.experiment: Compute 1D analytical azimuthal dust drift-mixing equilibrium profiles (Birnstiel et al. 2013) and run a 2D PLUTO hydrodynamics simulation of a Rossby-wave-unstable cavity edge with six dust fluids.
claims.result: The 1D analytical model qualitatively matches the azimuthal peak profile at 137 au (for A_gas=1.1, sigma_y=75 deg, alpha=5e-4) but not the trailing tail; the 2D PLUTO simulation forms a coalesced massive vortex whose synthetic 230 GHz image reproduces the general ring/cavity morphology and a mild asymmetry between leading and trailing sides.
claims.finding: The vortex dust-trapping scenario is a plausible explanation for the observed high-contrast crescent and asymmetric tail, although parameter degeneracies and alternative mechanisms (such as binary-induced horseshoes or infalling streamers) remain.

evidence.quote: We then run a hydrodynamic model of a vortex with different dust fluids, reproducing the general morphology observed in the HD 34700A and IRS 48 systems, with the emission around the vortex showing a mild asymmetry between the leading and trailing sides.
In combination with the above point, this suggests that the vortex scenario is indeed a plausible explanation for these features.

claims.hypothesis: The dust ring around HD 34700A is eccentric, as suggested by the offset of the inner disc emission from the ring centre and the non-horizontal polar deprojection.
claims.experiment: Expand the galario visibility model to parameterize the ring and arc radii as an ellipse with eccentricity e and argument of periastron omega, and fit with emcee.
claims.result: The HD 34700A fit converges to e = 0.109 (+0.005/-0.004) and a = 529 (+/-3) mas, while IRS 48 and HD 142527 fail to converge; however, the residual images for the circular and eccentric models of HD 34700A show no substantial difference.
claims.finding: Because of degeneracy between the circular and eccentric models, the visibility fit does not confirm whether the disc around HD 34700A is eccentric or circular.

evidence.quote: The HD 34700 A model converges to a solution with $a = 529^{+3}_{-3}~\rm mas$, $e = 0.109^{+0.005}_{-0.004}$, $\omega = 105^{+7}_{-7}~ \rm deg$, $\Delta\rm RA = 99.6^{+0.6}_{-0.3}~\mu as$, $\Delta\rm Dec = 19^{+6}_{-5}~\mu as$
However, the model show a degeneracy with the circular solution, thus our estimates do not confirm that the system is eccentric.

why_this_data.value: New high-resolution (0.11'') ALMA Band 6 continuum observations of HD 34700A resolved the ring, cavity, and high-contrast crescent co-located with a tentative kinematic vortex signature, motivating comparison with the two highest-contrast transition discs (IRS 48 and HD 142527).

evidence.quote: In this paper, we present recent ALMA observations of the system HD 34700 AaAb (hereafter HD 34700 A) that resolved a prominent dust asymmetry co-located with a tentative kinematic vortex signature (cite: Stadler_2026).

We focus on the continuum data of HD 34700 A and perform visibility modelling of the new ALMA Band 6 observations, comparing it with the transition discs with the most prominent asymmetries (with a contrast $\gtrsim30$) from the (cite: vdM2021) sample, namely Oph-IRS 48 (IRS 48 hereafter) and HD 142527.

why_this_method.value: Visibility modelling with galario and asymmetric Gaussian arcs (plus two arcs for HD 142527) was chosen because previous single-arc models left up to 40% residuals in HD 142527 and did not account for the resolved ring in IRS 48 or the asymmetric trailing tails.

evidence.quote: However, recent observations of IRS 48 also resolve a ring, while a single arc could not fully describe the double peaked emission of HD 142527, as shown by their intensity residuals of up to $40\%$.

We use asymmetric arcs with different azimuthal widths on the left ($\sigma_{\theta,\rm l}$) and right ($\sigma_{\theta,\rm r}$) of the peak intensity to better reproduce the tail observed in the continuum images.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Orbit clustering in an eccentric disc (rejected due to observed azimuthal contrasts >> 5)

evidence.quote: The high azimuthal contrast of the asymmetries rules out the orbit clustering of eccentric cavities scenario (cite: Ataiee2013).

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Binary-disc interaction alone carving the large cavities in HD 34700A and HD 142527 (rejected because binary separations of 0.69 au and 10.8 au can only carve cavities up to ~6 a_bin)

evidence.quote: However, with a binary separation of $0.69~\rm au$ for HD 34700 A (cite: Sterzik2005) and $10.8~\rm au$ for HD 142527 (cite: Nowak2024), the observed cavity sizes are too large to be explained by binary interaction alone, as shown by the simulations of HD 142527 in (cite: Penzlin2024).

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Unfixed central Gaussian in HD 34700A and inner Gaussian component in IRS 48 visibility models (rejected because the Gaussian merges with the ring in HD 34700A and fails to recover inner disc emission in IRS 48)

evidence.quote: We choose to fix the inner Gaussian to the image centre for the HD 34700 A model due to its proximity to the ring asymmetry, as the inner Gaussian would merge with the ring otherwise.
In the case of IRS 48, adding a Gaussian component to the model does not recover the emission from the inner disc.

limitations_admitted.value: The 1D analytical dust trapping model has a highly degenerate parameter space and does not reproduce the elongated trailing tail.

evidence.quote: While this set of parameters results in a model matching the observed intensity azimuthal profile on a qualitative level, it should not be taken as a unique solution.

Although this model can reproduce qualitatively the observed intensity azimuthal profile of the peak emission for the HD 34700 A system, it does not recover the elongated trailing tail that we see in Fig.1 and 4.

limitations_admitted.value: The 2D PLUTO hydrodynamic model is a rescalable proof-of-concept with an aspect ratio profile somewhat high for a passively irradiated disc around HD 34700A, so it does not uniquely constrain exact gas or dust properties.

evidence.loc: Dust distribution around a massive vortex
evidence.quote: Our profile for $h$ is quite in line with expectations beyond 100 au for typical disc parameters, even if possibly rather unrealistic for a passively irradiated disc with the particular stellar parameters for HD 34700 A.

evidence.loc: Dust distribution around a massive vortex
evidence.quote: As a result, this model does not necessarily constrain the exact gas or dust properties around HD 34700 A beyond highlighting the requirement for large grains trapped in the vortex, which was already inferred in Sect. 5.1.

limitations_admitted.value: Eccentric galario visibility models fail to converge for IRS 48 and HD 142527 and are degenerate with the circular model for HD 34700A.

evidence.quote: In the cases of IRS 48 and HD 142527, the eccentric `galario` models do not reach convergence.
This suggests that there is a degeneracy between the circular and eccentric model, and it is currently unclear if the disc around HD 34700 A is circular or eccentric.

limitations_admitted.value: Single-wavelength continuum data cannot definitively distinguish between an anticyclonic vortex, a binary-induced gas horseshoe, or streamer-triggered vortices without higher angular resolution kinematics and multi-wavelength continuum observations.

evidence.quote: However, it is currently unclear which physical mechanism is causing the observed azimuthal asymmetric rings in the discs of HD 34700 A, IRS 48 and HD 142527.
In order to differentiate between the two scenarios, higher spatial resolution ($\lesssim0.1\ensuremath{''}$) observations are needed to detect the rotational kinematic pattern of a vortex.
